beats.narration_text: Euler's formula and the unit circle.

Theta sweeps from zero to two-pi. The point on the unit circle follows. Its horizontal projection onto the real axis traces out a cosine wave. Its vertical projection onto the imaginary axis traces out a sine wave. Both projections running simultaneously, driven by a single complex exponential rotating at unit speed.

This is why complex exponentials appear everywhere in wave physics. A wave e to the i-omega-t is a point rotating in the complex plane at angular frequency omega. Its real part is the physical oscillation. The complex representation carries phase information and makes superposition trivial.

lines: Phase lives in the imaginary part.

beats.narration_text: Euler's formula: e to the i-theta equals cosine theta plus i times sine theta. The special case theta equals pi gives e to the i-pi plus one equals zero — connecting e, i, pi, one, and zero in one identity. The general form is the foundation of Fourier analysis and all of wave mechanics.

lines: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ

beats.narration_text: e to the i-theta equals cosine theta plus i sine theta. As theta sweeps, the point traces the unit circle. Real part: cosine. Imaginary part: sine. This unifies complex exponentials, trigonometry, and the wave equation — and it is what the animation shows, computed from the formula.
